abstract: Belowground root inputs contribute to stable soil organic carbon (SOC) significantly more than aboveground plant inputs. Yet, current understanding of the role of belowground root herbivory in ecosystem C cycling is remarkably weaker than that of aboveground herbivory and litter inputs. Here, we experimentally exposed roots of co-occurring mature hickory (Carya) and maple (Acer) trees, in a temperate hardwood forest, to increasing herbivory pressure by ubiquitous root-feeding soil nematodes. We investigated responses and underlying mechanisms of root C exudation as well as downstream indirect effects of root herbivory on mineral-associated organic carbon (MAOC) pools. Increased root herbivory promoted C exudation, which was strongly associated with increasing root necrosis and resulted in indirect positive effects on MAOC. Importantly, these direct and indirect effects were larger in magnitude and only significant in hickory but not maple. Instead, the latter appeared to channel herbivory response toward diversified chemical defense signaling rather than bulk exudate release, while more extensive root damage and increased exudation rate with less compositional change of hickory suggested a greater role of passive exudate release through leaking wounds in roots. Taken together, these findings indicate divergent eco-physiological mechanisms and ecosystem C consequences of root herbivory in mature hickory and maple trees, and show that changes in exudate quantity rather than chemical composition impact soil C. This study extends field-based causal explanation of root C inputs and retention in soil by highlighting the role of root-feeding animals in regulating rhizodeposition, and offers a basis for integrating belowground herbivory into multitrophic biogeochemistry.
